"Our analysis applies to illegal aliens as well as to legal residents and citizens. The United States Constitution provides due process protections to all persons," he wrote, emphasizing "all." Barletta said he would "continue to fight for the people of this community and other cities around the country." “This fight is far from over,” he told reporters outside the courtroom. “Hazleton is not going to back down. ... We will take it all the way to the Supreme Court if we have to.”

Barletta drafted the act last year after what he described on his Web site, www.smalltowndefenders.com, as “a high-profile murder, the discharge of a gun at a crowded city playground, and drug busts” allegedly involving undocumented immigrants.

“Illegal aliens in our city create an economic burden that threatens our quality of life,” he wrote. “With a growing problem and a limited budget, I could not sit back any longer and allow this to happen. I needed to act!”

Hazleton’s population was 23,000 in 2000. Since then, it has grown to an estimated 30,000 to 33,000, with many of the newcomers being Mexican immigrants, according to Munley.

The American Civil Liberties Union of Pennsylvania was among several groups that filed the lawsuit on behalf of Hazleton residents, landlords, and business owners. The groups argued that only the federal government has the authority to regulate immigration or to deprive residents of equal protection rights. They also said the ordinances violated state and federal housing laws.

Munley said the ordinances “penalize landlords, tenants, employers and employees without providing them the procedural protections required by federal law, including notice and an opportunity to be heard.”

“Our analysis applies to illegal aliens as well as to legal residents and citizens. The United States Constitution provides due process protections to all persons,” he wrote, emphasizing “all.”

Munley, whom President Clinton appointed to the federal bench in 1998, wrote that the city exceeded its police powers by enacting unconstitutional ordinances.

Barletta said he would “continue to fight for the people of this community and other cities around the country.”

“It’s almost amusing to me that the judge would say we can’t do what the federal government should be doing, when in fact the federal government is not doing their job,” he told CNN’s Lou Dobbs.

**Federal judge blocks Hazleton immigration ordinances, ruling city overstepped into federal law**

**SCRANTON, Pa.** — A federal judge on Thursday struck down the City of Hazleton’s controversial immigration ordinances, ruling that the northeastern Pennsylvania city violated the U.S. Constitution by trying to punish landlords and employers who dealt with undocumented immigrants.

U.S. District Judge **James M. Munley** issued a broad decision blocking enforcement of Hazleton’s **Illegal Immigration Relief Act** and related rental ordinances, finding that the city had intruded into an area reserved for the federal government and created procedures that failed to protect basic due process rights.

The ordinances, championed by Hazleton Mayor **Lou Barletta**, would have penalized businesses that hired undocumented immigrants and landlords who rented to them. The measures also required tenants to obtain rental permits and empowered city officials to investigate immigration status based on complaints.

Munley concluded that, however serious Hazleton officials believed their local problems to be, the city could not create its own immigration enforcement system.

“Hazleton, in its zeal to control the presence of a group deemed undesirable, violated the rights of such people, as well as others within the community,” Munley wrote in substance, emphasizing that immigration regulation is a federal responsibility.

## Supremacy Clause: federal law controls immigration

At the heart of the decision was the **Supremacy Clause** of the U.S. Constitution, which provides that federal law is the “supreme Law of the Land.” Under that principle, state and local governments may not enact laws that conflict with federal statutes or interfere with federal authority.

Munley ruled that Hazleton’s ordinances were **preempted** by federal immigration law. Congress has already created a detailed national framework for determining immigration status, regulating employment of noncitizens, and deciding when and how immigration violations are handled.

The judge found that Hazleton’s local scheme would have disrupted that framework by placing city officials in the role of immigration adjudicators and creating local penalties on top of federal law. Even if Hazleton’s policy goals mirrored federal concerns, Munley said the city could not impose its own separate enforcement regime.

The court’s reasoning reflected a central constitutional concern: if every municipality adopted its own immigration rules, immigration policy would become fragmented from city to city, undermining the uniform national system the Constitution assigns to the federal government.

## Due process concerns for landlords, tenants and employers

Munley also raised serious **due process** concerns.

The ordinances allowed complaints to trigger investigations against landlords and businesses accused of renting to or employing undocumented immigrants. But the court found the procedures were flawed because they did not provide adequate safeguards before licenses could be suspended or penalties imposed.

For landlords and tenants, the rental provisions created the possibility that people could lose housing based on uncertain or mistaken determinations of immigration status. Businesses also faced penalties based on processes that Munley found insufficiently protective of their rights.

The judge noted that determining immigration status is often complex. A person’s status may depend on pending applications, federal discretion, changing documentation, or other factors that local officials are not equipped to evaluate. Because the ordinances could lead to serious consequences without reliable procedures, the court found they posed constitutional problems.

Civil-rights groups also argued that the laws would encourage discrimination against Latino residents and immigrants regardless of legal status, because landlords and employers might avoid anyone they feared could bring scrutiny or penalties.

## Barletta vows appeal

Mayor **Lou Barletta**, who became a national figure among supporters of tougher local immigration enforcement, criticized the ruling and said Hazleton would appeal.

Barletta had argued that the ordinances were necessary because illegal immigration had strained city resources and contributed to crime and economic problems. He maintained that Hazleton was not trying to deport anyone, but only to deny business licenses to employers who hired undocumented workers and rental permits to landlords who housed them.

Following the ruling, Barletta said the city would continue fighting, signaling an appeal to the **U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit**. Supporters of the ordinances framed the case as a test of whether local governments could act when they believed federal immigration enforcement was inadequate.

## ACLU hails decision

The **American Civil Liberties Union**, which helped challenge the ordinances along with other civil-rights organizations, praised Munley’s ruling as a major victory.

ACLU lawyers said the decision confirmed that cities cannot write their own immigration codes or punish residents based on a locally run immigration-enforcement process. They also said the ruling protected not only immigrants, but landlords, employers, families and lawful residents who could be swept up in discriminatory enforcement.

The ACLU and its allies argued throughout the case that Hazleton’s ordinances would make Latino residents targets of suspicion, discourage people from renting to immigrants, and create fear throughout the community. After the ruling, civil-rights advocates said the court had sent a clear message to other municipalities considering similar laws: immigration enforcement must remain consistent with federal law and constitutional protections.

## A closely watched national case

Hazleton’s ordinances drew national attention because they were among the most prominent local attempts to crack down on undocumented immigration during a period when many cities and towns were debating similar measures.

Munley’s ruling did not deny that local governments may face real challenges connected to immigration. But the decision made clear that cities must operate within constitutional limits.

The case became a landmark in the broader legal fight over local immigration ordinances, with Hazleton serving as a symbol for both sides: supporters saw it as a city trying to defend itself, while opponents saw it as an unconstitutional attempt to turn local officials, landlords and employers into immigration agents.
